title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: A great hardware company sells a chip once; a great platform company turns every developer's keyboard into a recurring tollbooth—until a governance or architectural shock tests whether the institution outlives its founder.
epigraph.author: Semiconductor Platform Forensics

web_blocks.html: NVIDIA was founded on April 5, 1993, in San Jose, California, by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem [20]. Their founding bet was that PCs would evolve from text processors into 3D graphics and multimedia machines. Early survival was anything but assured. The company's first chip, the NV1 (1995), used quadratic texture mapping—a dead-end standard that Microsoft's Direct3D rejected—and its follow-on NV2 failed to ship [20]. By 1997, NVIDIA was weeks from running out of cash before betting its remaining capital on the RIVA 128, which shipped over one million units in four months and rescued the firm [20]. Two years later, in 1999, NVIDIA went public on January 22 and launched the GeForce 256, integrating hardware transform and lighting (T&L) onto a single chip and coining the term GPU [20].

Between 2000 and 2026, NVIDIA's corporate evolution unfolded across four distinct operational cycles, each marked by severe drawdowns that forged its current full-stack architecture. The first crisis struck in 2008: defective underfill packaging on mobile GeForce 8 GPUs ('Bumpgate') triggered massive warranty charges just as the Global Financial Crisis froze PC demand [20]. Simultaneously, Huang committed R&D capital to CUDA (launched in 2006), a parallel-computing software layer that let researchers program GPUs in C/C++ for non-graphics math. Wall Street initially panned CUDA as a margin drag, yet it quietly seeded two decades of developer lock-in.

web_blocks.takeaway: Every major NVIDIA hardware crisis—from 1997 NV1 to 2018 crypto and 2022 gaming inventory gluts—forced deeper vertical integration into software (CUDA) and networking (Mellanox/NVLink), culminating in the November 2026 test of whether that institutional machine outlives its co-founder.

web_blocks.html: The second and third cycles exposed NVIDIA's historical vulnerability to consumer and crypto boom-busts. In 2018, Ethereum mining inflated GeForce demand before crashing, leaving channel partners awash in used GPUs and pushing FY2020 revenue down 6.8% to $10.92 billion [18]. A similar pandemic-era PC and crypto surge ended in 2022 (FY2023), when gaming inventory gluts forced steep channel price cuts and halved GAAP operating income from $10.04 billion in FY22 to $4.22 billion in FY23 [19]. Crucially, during that exact downturn, NVIDIA closed its $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox (2020) and launched the Hopper H100 architecture, shifting its center of gravity from PC graphics cards to rack-scale AI clusters.

The fourth cycle—from FY2024 through Q3 FY2027—produced the fastest industrial scaling in modern semiconductor history, alongside an abrupt leadership shock. Revenue exploded from $26.97 billion in FY23 to $60.92 billion in FY24, $130.50 billion in FY25, and $215.94 billion in FY26 [4, 18]. In Q3 FY27 (ended October 25, 2026), quarterly revenue alone reached $115.8 billion (+103% YoY), propelled by Blackwell and the debut of the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale platform (~$20 billion in first-quarter shipments) [1, 6]. Yet on November 12, 2026—five days before Q3 earnings—co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO, and director following disclosures of personal conduct violations [5, 6]. Longtime CFO Colette Kress stepped in as Interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones became NVIDIA's first independent Board Chair, and the Board formed a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee [5, 7].

web_blocks.title: Institutional Stress Test: Post-Founder Governance Transition (Nov 2026)
paragraphs: For 33 years, Jensen Huang was NVIDIA's chief architect, chief evangelist, and cultural anchor. His November 12, 2026 resignation—with the Board explicitly ruling out reinstatement [6]—removes the industry's most influential founder-CEO right as NVIDIA scales $390 billion in supply commitments and navigates tightening U.S. export controls [7, 9]. While Kress provides financial continuity and deep operational command, the permanent CEO search is a defining governance inflection.

book_paragraphs: If you and I want to understand how a company founded at a San Jose Denny's in 1993 ended up generating $115.8 billion in a single quarter thirteen years after the smartphone era began, we have to look past the silicon and study how NVIDIA survived its own near-death experiences. Most investors today see NVIDIA as an unstoppable AI juggernaut. In truth, its thirty-three-year history is a study in violent cycles—and in the rare discipline to use downturns to widen its moat while rivals cut R&D.

Start in 1997. NVIDIA's very first chip, the NV1, was an engineering curiosity that bet on the wrong 3D math—quadratic texture mapping—just as Microsoft standardized PC gaming on triangles via Direct3D. The follow-up NV2 never shipped. With only weeks of payroll left in the bank, Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem bet the company on the RIVA 128. It worked, selling over a million units in four months, and set up NVIDIA's January 1999 IPO and the launch of the GeForce 256 later that year.

What happened next is the real secret to NVIDIA's durability. In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA, a software toolkit that let scientists and engineers use GPUs for general-purpose parallel computing. Two years later, when the 2008 financial crisis collided with 'Bumpgate'—a costly laptop GPU packaging defect—analysts begged management to slash CUDA spending to protect short-term margins. Huang refused. That stubborn decision meant that when AlexNet proved in 2012 that deep neural networks trained dramatically faster on GPUs than CPUs, CUDA was already sitting on university servers around the world.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Every semiconductor boom eventually meets an inventory hangover—NVIDIA proved that in 2018 and again in 2022. What separates NVIDIA from ordinary chipmakers is that it spent its 2020–2022 cash flows buying Mellanox and building full-rack systems, turning a cyclical GPU business into an integrated data-center platform. Now, after Jensen Huang's November 2026 departure, you and I have to ask whether that platform runs on institutional muscle or founder magic.

book_subsections.title: From Crypto Hangovers to Rack-Scale Dominance (2018–2026)
paragraphs: Walk through the two pre-AI busts with me, because they explain why seasoned chip analysts still watch NVIDIA's channel inventories like hawks. In 2018, cryptocurrency miners snapped up GeForce cards at inflated prices, only to dump them onto secondary markets when Ethereum crashed. NVIDIA's revenue dipped nearly 7% in FY2020. Four years later, in 2022, pandemic PC demand cooled just as crypto collapsed again, forcing NVIDIA to write down gaming inventory and cutting operating income by more than half in FY2023.

Yet beneath that messy gaming reset, NVIDIA had already closed its $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox in 2020, securing high-speed InfiniBand networking. When generative AI exploded in early 2023, NVIDIA wasn't just selling a standalone graphics chip; it was selling entire interconnected clusters—GPUs, NVLink switches, InfiniBand fabrics, and CUDA libraries—that hyperscalers could deploy out of the box. Revenue leaped from $26.97 billion in FY23 to $215.94 billion in FY26.

book_subsections.title: November 2026: The Post-Jensen Era Begins
paragraphs: That brings us to the watershed moment of November 2026. Just five days before NVIDIA reported $115.8 billion in Q3 FY27 revenue—and nearly $20 billion from the debut quarter of its Vera Rubin NVL72 racks—co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 over personal conduct violations. Longtime CFO Colette Kress stepped in as Interim CEO, and Harvey Jones became NVIDIA's first independent Board Chair.

The timing is extraordinary: operationally, NVIDIA's engineering cadence has never been faster, yet culturally and strategically, the company must now prove to customers, suppliers like TSMC and SK Hynix, and its 42,000 employees that its multi-year roadmap doesn't depend on one person in a leather jacket.

For institutional investors, that distinction is everything. In 1997, 2008, 2018, and 2022, NVIDIA survived because a founder-led engineering culture could pivot overnight without boardroom paralysis. Now, under Interim CEO Colette Kress and independent Chair Harvey Jones—with a newly minted National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee—NVIDIA must demonstrate that its architectural cadence, CUDA ecosystem, and rack-scale execution are durable institutional habits rather than one founder's personal willpower.
